h1: The 6 Best Toshiba Microwaves of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six Toshiba microwaves compared on capacity, wattage, inverter, smart sensor and air fry features to help you choose.
summary: The Toshiba ML-EM45PIT is the best Toshiba microwave here, the only one pairing inverter, smart sensor and auto defrost in a 1.6 cu ft cavity. The 1200W Smart Sensor model gives most of that for a bucket less. The flatbed suits inverter fans, and the 0.9 cu ft model covers dorms.
intro: Toshiba sells many microwaves under near-identical names, and the biggest trap is assuming two listings called Countertop Microwave Oven are the same machine. They are not, and the listing title rarely says so. A 1.2 cu ft model at 1000W cooks and fits very differently from a 1.6 cu ft model at 1200W, even when the product photos look alike.

We reviewed eight Toshiba listings and ranked six distinct models on the spec sheet: capacity, wattage, smart sensor, inverter, air fry function and price bucket. Where two listings looked identical we counted them once. The real decision is not brand, since you have already chosen it, but which of three upgrades you actually want: inverter, sensor or size, and what each costs in price bucket.

products.name: TOSHIBA ML-EM45PIT(SS) Countertop Microwave Oven with Inverter
products.verdict: Inverter, smart sensor and auto defrost in a 1.6 cu ft body.
products.description:
The ML-EM45PIT is a stainless Toshiba with inverter technology, smart sensor, auto defrost and a 1.6 cu ft interior. Inverter delivers steady power instead of cycling full power on and off, which is why it is better at defrosting and reheating food that would otherwise end up hot at the edges and cold in the middle. The sensor removes the guessing on timing.

It takes first place because no other Toshiba here lists all three of those cooking features together. The 1200W Smart Sensor model beats it on listed wattage and price bucket, but gives up the inverter and defrost. That inverter and defrost pairing is what justifies the move up to the $200 to $500 tier.

Buy it for large dishes and frequent defrosting. The caveat is that the listing never states wattage, so the power figure you would compare is missing.
products.idealFor: Cooks wanting automatic settings and larger dishes.

products.name: TOSHIBA Microwave Oven with Smart Sensor
products.verdict: 1.6 cu ft, 1200W and a smart sensor for $100-200.
products.description:
This Toshiba combines 1.6 cu ft of capacity, 1200W and a smart sensor, in the $100 to $200 range. Wattage is the main driver of heating speed, and 1200W is as high as any Toshiba here goes. The sensor reads steam so rice, vegetables and leftovers need less manual time adjustment.

It ranks second because it matches the ML-EM45PIT on size and sensor while costing a full bucket less. What it gives up is the inverter and any auto defrost listing, so thawing a frozen roast will be the place you notice. Against the flatbed, it offers a larger cavity (1.6 against 1.3 cu ft) at the same price bucket.

Buy it for a family that wants space and speed without top pricing. The caveat is cooking quality at low power settings, since no inverter is listed.
products.idealFor: Families wanting power and space for less.

products.name: TOSHIBA Flatbed Microwave Oven with Inverter Technology
products.verdict: A flatbed 1.3 cu ft inverter model at 1200W.
products.description:
Toshiba's flatbed removes the turntable entirely, so the floor is one flat surface. Inside it is a 1.3 cu ft inverter model rated at 1200W, priced $100 to $200. A flat floor lets a rectangular dish use every corner, and wiping the cavity takes one pass.

It ranks third because the interior is 0.3 cu ft smaller than the two 1.6 cu ft Toshibas, and the listing shows no smart sensor. But it is the cheapest route to inverter cooking here, and that beats the 1.2 cu ft sensor model below it on power by 200W.

Buy it if you want steady inverter power and easy cleaning. The caveat is dish size: a 1.3 cu ft cavity will not fit a large casserole as comfortably as the 1.6 cu ft models above.
products.idealFor: Buyers wanting inverter cooking for less.

products.name: TOSHIBA Countertop Microwave Oven with Smart Sensor
products.verdict: A 1.2 cu ft, 1000W model with a smart sensor.
products.description:
This Toshiba pairs a smart sensor with a 1.2 cu ft cavity and 1000W, in the $100 to $200 range. The sensor is the reason to own it over a basic model: it detects steam and adjusts time, which prevents overcooked edges on leftovers and rubbery reheated rice.

It ranks fourth because it has a smaller cavity than the 1.6 cu ft sensor model and gives up 200W against both the flatbed and that model, at the same price bucket. If you wanted a sensor, the larger one costs no more. Its edge over the 0.9 cu ft base model is the sensor itself and 0.3 cu ft more space.

Buy it for a couple or small household that wants automatic settings in a mid-size body. The caveat is power: 1000W means longer heating times than any 1200W Toshiba here.
products.idealFor: Couples wanting a sensor at mid-size.

products.name: TOSHIBA Air Fryer Combo Microwave
products.verdict: A 1.0 cu ft microwave that also air fries.
products.description:
The Air Fryer Combo is a 1.0 cu ft Toshiba that microwaves and air fries, priced $100 to $200. Combining the two functions saves a whole appliance footprint in a small kitchen, and crisping is something no plain microwave here can do.

It ranks fifth because the cavity is only 1.0 cu ft and the listing gives no wattage. Combo units compromise on both functions, so you pay for flexibility rather than the best microwave. Against the 0.9 cu ft base model it adds crisping for a higher bucket, and against the 1.2 cu ft sensor model it gives up space and a sensor.

Buy it if counter space is the constraint. The caveat is capacity: whole-chicken or family-size air frying will not fit, so confirm the basket size on the full listing.

products.name: TOSHIBA Microwave Oven
products.description:
The base Toshiba is a 0.9 cu ft, 900W microwave in the $50 to $100 bucket. It does the basic job of reheating coffee, soup and frozen meals, and that is all it is designed to do. The small footprint also suits shelves and desks.

It ranks last because capacity and power are the lowest of the six, and no sensor or inverter is listed. At 900W it takes longer than the 1200W models, and 0.9 cu ft limits plate size. But it is the cheapest by a full bucket, and for many offices that settles it.

Buy it for a dorm room, break room or guest room. The caveat is dish fit: check that your largest plate rotates freely before ordering, since 0.9 cu ft leaves little clearance.

whatMatters.detail: An inverter microwave supplies steady lower power instead of switching full power on and off. That tends to heat more evenly and defrost without cooking the edges. Two Toshibas here list it, the ML-EM45PIT and the flatbed. Confirm the word inverter in the title, not just in marketing images.

A smart sensor detects steam released by food and adjusts cooking time for you. It matters most for reheating and vegetables, where guessing causes rubbery or cold spots. Several Toshibas here list it, including the 1.2 and 1.6 cu ft models. Check for smart sensor in the title or bullets and for dedicated sensor menu buttons.

Capacity runs from 0.9 to 1.6 cu ft here. Interior volume decides whether a 12 inch plate or casserole can turn freely. A bigger cavity also needs more counter and a clear vent. Measure your largest dish and your counter space, then compare with the listing before choosing. Do not assume the cu ft number in the title applies to usable turntable room.

Wattage drives heating speed. Toshiba models here range from 900W to 1200W, so a frozen dinner can take noticeably longer on the smallest. Some listings, like the ML-EM45PIT and the Air Fryer Combo, omit it. If the figure is missing, check the manufacturer's spec page before assuming the power matches a similar model.

Two designs break from the standard microwave. A flatbed has no turntable, giving a flat floor that is easier to clean and fits rectangular dishes. An air fry combo adds crisping to a 1.0 cu ft cavity. Decide whether you want either. The feature name appears in the title, so confirm it there.

faq.a: The ML-EM45PIT and the 1200W Smart Sensor model both list 1.6 cu ft, the largest Toshiba cavity here. The flatbed follows at 1.3 cu ft, and the dorm model is smallest at 0.9.

Assuming identically named Toshibas are the same machine. The 1000W Smart Sensor model and the 1200W one share a name pattern but differ in capacity and power, so read wattage and cu ft before buying.

faq.q: Is the inverter worth the extra?
faq.a: If you want steady power plus auto defrost in one body, yes. The ML-EM45PIT combines both. If you mostly reheat, the 1.6 cu ft Smart Sensor model costs a bucket less and still handles it well.

faq.q: How do I use smart sensor settings?
faq.a: Open the sensor menu, pick the food category and let the microwave detect steam to set the time. Do not open the door early, since that interrupts the steam reading. The manual lists which food categories each Toshiba supports, so check it for yours.

faq.q: How do I clean a flatbed microwave?
faq.a: Wipe the flat floor with a damp cloth once it cools. The Toshiba flatbed has no turntable or roller ring to remove, so spills are easier to clear than in standard models with a rotating plate.

faq.q: Does the air fryer combo replace an air fryer?
faq.a: Partly. The 1.0 cu ft combo adds air frying to a microwave, but small capacity limits batch size. A dedicated air fryer handles larger loads, so treat the combo as a space saver.

finalTake: Buy the ML-EM45PIT if you want every automatic feature in a full size cavity. Most families will be just as happy with the 1.6 cu ft, 1200W Smart Sensor model at a lower bucket. Take the flatbed for an inverter without a turntable, the combo for air frying, and the 900W model only for a dorm or office.
